title: Pot-au-Feu
subtitle: French boiled beef and vegetables in broth
excerpt: Pot-au-feu is the national dish of France: a pot of beef, marrow bones, and root vegetables simmered gently together for hours until the broth is clear and golden. The broth is served first as a soup. Then the beef and vegetables follow. It is the simplest and most fundamental dish of French home cooking -- little technique, but long patience.
sourceNotes: Pot-au-feu (pot on the fire) is considered the national dish of France. It has been eaten in French homes since at least the 17th century. The dish requires no special technique -- only good ingredients and time. Traditionally served in three acts: the broth, the vegetables, and the meat. Marrow bones are optional but traditional and add enormous richness to the broth.

recipe.freezeNotes: The broth freezes very well. Meat and vegetables are best eaten fresh.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The broth improves overnight. Refrigerate and remove the fat layer before reheating.

content.text: The beef goes into cold water, not boiling water. Starting cold draws out the proteins slowly into the broth, giving a cleaner, clearer result. The broth should barely simmer -- a rolling boil makes it cloudy and the meat tough. Skim frequently in the first hour.

content.text: Put {{beef-shin}} beef shin in a very large pot. Cover with 3.5 litres of cold water and {{beef-stock}} stock. Bring very slowly to a boil over medium-low heat, about 30 minutes. Skim the grey foam from the surface frequently.

Add {{onion}} charred onion, {{garlic}} garlic, {{thyme-fresh}} thyme, {{bay-leaves}} bay leaves, {{black-peppercorns}} peppercorns, and {{salt-table}} salt. Reduce to the lowest simmer. Cook for 2 hours.

Add {{carrots}} carrots, {{leek}} leek, {{celery}} celery, and {{turnip}} turnip. Continue simmering for 40 minutes. Add {{potatoes-waxy}} potatoes and cook for a further 20 minutes until everything is tender.

Ladle the broth into bowls and serve as a starter. Then plate the vegetables and sliced beef together. Serve with {{dijon-mustard}} Dijon mustard, coarse {{sea-salt-flakes}} salt, and pickled gherkins.

items.symptom: The broth is cloudy and grey
items.cause: It boiled rather than simmered, or not enough skimming was done.
items.fix: A cloudy pot-au-feu still tastes good. Next time, start with cold water, skim constantly in the first 45 minutes, and keep the heat as low as possible throughout. A bare simmer -- a few bubbles at the edge -- is correct.

content.text: Pot-au-feu is described by the gastronome Curnonsky as the national dish of France. It has been the cornerstone of French home cooking for centuries and is a close relative of the Spanish cocido, Italian bollito misto, and British boiled beef and carrots. The dish is made across all regions of France. It is not a restaurant dish -- it belongs to the home kitchen and to winter.
